content: The Cow Parsnip, scientifically known as Heracleum maximum and also referred to as Indian Celery or Pushki, is the only species of the Hogweed genus that is native to North America. Its taxonomic classification has been a subject of debate, with various authoritative sources identifying it as Heracleum maximum, Heracleum lanatum, H. linatum, or as a subspecies (H. sphondylium subsp. montanum) or variety (H. sphondylium var. linatum) of the Common Hogweed (H. sphondylium). The classification used here aligns with the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS). This plant is distributed widely across North America, spanning from coast to coast. Within the continental United States, it is absent only in the southeastern states, from Texas eastward. In the western regions, it extends as far north as Alaska and throughout most of Canada. It thrives at altitudes of up to 2,500 meters. While the Cow Parsnip is generally abundant and not considered a conservation concern, its population is declining in certain areas. For instance, it is classified as endangered in Kentucky, whereas in some western regions, it is regarded as an invasive weed. The Cow Parsnip is a tall herbaceous plant that can grow to heights exceeding two meters. It belongs to the carrot family (Apiaceae) and features characteristic flower umbels that are approximately 20 centimeters in diameter. These umbels may appear flat-topped or more rounded but are consistently white in color. The plant’s leaves are large, reaching up to 40 centimeters across, and are divided into lobes. Its stems are thick and succulent. The Cow Parsnip is considered a problematic weed, particularly in pastures, where it can negatively affect the quality of milk produced by cows that consume it. Despite its toxic properties, various Native American groups historically utilized this plant for numerous purposes. Different parts of the plant were used by different tribes. One of the most common applications was the preparation of poultices to treat bruises or sores. Additionally, the young stalks and leaf stems, harvested before the plant reached maturity, were consumed as food after peeling off the outer skin, which revealed a sweet flavor. The dried stems were repurposed as drinking straws for the elderly or infirm and were also used to craft flutes for children. The roots of the plant can be used to produce a yellow dye, and an infusion made from the flowers was traditionally applied to the skin as a natural repellent against flies and mosquitoes.
